input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-539: Seminar in Artificial Intelligence. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Artificial Intelligence. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Artificial Intelligence cluster, the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Lecture 3

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-539]
This course examines current topics in Artificial Intelligence. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Artificial Intelligence cluster, the Computer Graphics and Visualization cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Lecture 3

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.example: Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk, ensuring clear ownership of risk management decisions.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern
beats.visualDirection: Show a four-step circular diagram labeled Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with arrows indicating the continuous cycle of risk management.

beats.claim: Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts to establish a baseline for risk analysis.
beats.example: A team maps a facial recognition system by documenting its intended use in public spaces, the affected population, and potential impacts on privacy and bias.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Map
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist template with fields for context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts, illustrating how to document risk context.

beats.claim: Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks, considering factors like data quality, uncertainty, robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and
beats.example: A team measures risk by running quantitative accuracy tests on training data and conducting qualitative interviews with stakeholders to assess fairness and transparency.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Measure
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen graphic: left side shows quantitative metrics (accuracy, precision, recall), right side shows qualitative indicators (stakeholder feedback, fairness audits, transparency reports).

beats.claim: Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring, ensuring ongoing oversight after deployment.
beats.example: A team prioritizes high-risk items, allocates budget for monitoring, and schedules regular audits to track system behavior and context changes.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage
beats.visualDirection: Display a risk prioritization matrix with quadrants for likelihood and impact, connected to a resource allocation table and a monitoring schedule.

beats.claim: Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation to ensure rigorous and reproducible results.
beats.example: A workflow separates raw data cleaning from model training, ensuring that validation and testing sets remain untouched during hyperparameter tuning.
beats.title: Machine-Learning Workflow Separation
beats.visualDirection: Show a linear pipeline diagram with six distinct stages: data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation, with arrows indicating the flow.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels.
beats.example: A supervised method classifies emails as spam or not using labeled data, whereas an unsupervised method clusters customer behavior without predefined categories.
beats.title: Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods
beats.visualDirection: Display two side-by-side examples: left shows labeled data points being mapped to classes, right shows unlabeled data points being grouped into clusters.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, ensuring that transformations do not inadvertently use information from validation or testing sets.
beats.example: A team fits a scaling transformer only on the training split, then applies the same transformation to validation and testing data to prevent data leakage.
beats.title: Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a data pipeline where a preprocessing step is applied only to the training set, with a warning icon indicating that fitting on other data causes leakage.

beats.claim: Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently, and cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits
beats.example: A pipeline ensures that scaling and imputation are applied identically to every fold during cross-validation, preventing inconsistent transformations across splits.
beats.title: Pipelines and Cross-Validation
beats.visualDirection: Display a pipeline object with preprocessing steps and an estimator, connected to a cross-validation loop showing multiple data splits being processed through the same pipeline.

beats.claim: Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors, and practitioners must verify that hyperparameter selection remains separate from final test evaluation to
beats.example: A team selects a metric like F1-score for an imbalanced classification task, ensuring that hyperparameter tuning does not influence the final test set evaluation.
beats.title: Evaluation Metrics and Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist with items: 'Metric matches task', 'Cost of errors considered', 'Hyperparameter selection separate from test evaluation', 'Leakage checked', 'Distribution shift assessed', 'Unexamined assumptions reviewed'.

input.text: With the foundation in place, examine how NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Map operates in a concrete sequence. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Consider this worked case: A team maps a facial recognition system by documenting its intended use in public spaces, the affected population, and potential impacts on privacy and bias. On screen, display a checklist template with fields for context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts, illustrating how to document risk context. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Use Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Consider this worked case: A team fits a scaling transformer only on the training split, then applies the same transformation to validation and testing data to prevent data leakage. On screen, show a diagram of a data pipeline where a preprocessing step is applied only to the training set, with a warning icon indicating that fitting on other data causes leakage. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Apply NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Consider this worked case: A team prioritizes high-risk items, allocates budget for monitoring, and schedules regular audits to track system behavior and context changes. On screen, display a risk prioritization matrix with quadrants for likelihood and impact, connected to a resource allocation table and a monitoring schedule. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

Now define NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Consider this worked case: Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk, ensuring clear ownership of risk management decisions. On screen, show a four-step circular diagram labeled Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with arrows indicating the continuous cycle of risk management. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.

Next, compare the choices involved in NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Measure and make the decision criteria explicit. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Consider this worked case: A team measures risk by running quantitative accuracy tests on training data and conducting qualitative interviews with stakeholders to assess fairness and transparency. On screen, show a split-screen graphic: left side shows quantitative metrics (accuracy, precision, recall), right side shows qualitative indicators (stakeholder feedback, fairness audits, transparency reports). Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

Stress-test the reasoning around Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Consider this worked case: A supervised method classifies emails as spam or not using labeled data, whereas an unsupervised method clusters customer behavior without predefined categories. On screen, display two side-by-side examples: left shows labeled data points being mapped to classes, right shows unlabeled data points being grouped into clusters. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

Begin by framing Course Scope and Faculty Flexibility as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Consider this worked case: A faculty member might propose a seminar focused on AI ethics, while another might focus on computer vision, each setting their own prerequisites and assessment methods. On screen, create an editable process diagram for Course Scope and Faculty Flexibility with labeled inputs, decisions, state changes, and a checked output. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

Examine the tradeoffs in Machine-Learning Workflow Separation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Consider this worked case: A workflow separates raw data cleaning from model training, ensuring that validation and testing sets remain untouched during hyperparameter tuning. On screen, show a linear pipeline diagram with six distinct stages: data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation, with arrows indicating the flow. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Finish with Evaluation Metrics and Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Consider this worked case: A team selects a metric like F1-score for an imbalanced classification task, ensuring that hyperparameter tuning does not influence the final test set evaluation. On screen, show a checklist with items: 'Metric matches task', 'Cost of errors considered', 'Hyperparameter selection separate from test evaluation', 'Leakage checked', 'Distribution shift assessed', 'Unexamined assumptions reviewed'. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

Connect Pipelines and Cross-Validation to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Consider this worked case: A pipeline ensures that scaling and imputation are applied identically to every fold during cross-validation, preventing inconsistent transformations across splits. On screen, display a pipeline object with preprocessing steps and an estimator, connected to a cross-validation loop showing multiple data splits being processed through the same pipeline. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
